passage:
Thursday
Today scared me. After PE, Dhruv was sitting on the changing-room bench, gasping and shaking, saying, "I can't breathe, I can't breathe." For a second I thought something terrible was happening to his heart, and my own hands went cold. I didn't know what to do, so I did what our coach once told us. I sat next to him, not too close, and talked slowly. "I'm here. You're breathing. Try breathing out long, like me." I asked the others to wait outside so it was quieter, and sent Anu to get Coach in case he needed a doctor. By the time Coach came, Dhruv's breathing was slower. Coach stayed with him and called his parents. Tonight he texted me: "Thanks for not leaving." I'm still shaky.
Kalyani

qa.q: Where was Dhruv sitting after PE?
qa.a: Dhruv was sitting on the changing-room bench.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when Dhruv said he couldn't breathe?
qa.a: Kalyani was frightened, fearing something terrible was happening to Dhruv's heart, and felt cold hands.

qa.q: Which of Kalyani's actions helped, and why?
qa.a: Staying near, talking slowly, clearing the room so it was quieter and sending for Coach in case a doctor was needed all kept Dhruv calmer and safer.

qa.q: What might Dhruv have felt when he texted "Thanks for not leaving"?
qa.a: Dhruv likely felt grateful and relieved that someone stayed beside him while he felt he could not breathe.

grounding: A friend sees someone gasping and shaking, fears something terrible is happening, and helps by staying near, speaking slowly, keeping it quiet and calling an adult.

subtype: Panic in a crowded or stressful place [Actor]
passage:
Dear Dolma,
You asked why I was so quiet on the phone on Monday. Here's the truth. On the 8:40 local to Churchgate, pressed between elbows and bags, I suddenly went hot all over. My fingers tingled, my chest locked tight, and every part of me screamed to get off, even though the train was moving. I honestly thought I'd faint.
Then I remembered what you told me after your exam-hall scare: breathe out slowly, hold something solid, and remind yourself it's a wave that rises and falls. So I gripped the metal pole, felt how cold it was, and counted my out-breaths. I told myself, this is the top of the wave. It will go down. By Dadar it had.
I'm going to see a doctor about it, like you did. Thank you for teaching me that.
Gautam

qa.q: What did Gautam grip on the train?
qa.a: Gautam gripped the metal pole.

qa.q: What did Gautam feel on the crowded local?
qa.a: Gautam felt terrified and trapped: hot all over, with tingling fingers, a locked chest and a desperate urge to get off.

qa.q: What helped Gautam ride out the panic until it passed?
qa.a: Slow out-breaths, holding the cold metal pole and remembering that the wave rises and then falls.

qa.q: How might Dolma feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Dolma may feel moved and glad that advice from Dolma's own exam-hall scare helped Gautam through it.

grounding: A young adult on a packed train feels heat, tingling, a tight chest and an urge to escape, and rides it out with slow breathing, something solid and the image of a wave.

passage: So, Tejas, you want the exam-hall story for the episode? Okay. Second-year finals, a hall with two hundred desks and none of the fans working. Ten minutes in, heat started in my neck and spread to my face. My hands tingled so much I dropped my pen. My chest felt like a belt was being tightened, and all I wanted was to run for the door. I'm Nikita, I'm usually the calm one, and I was sure I was about to faint in front of everyone. What saved me was simple. I pressed both palms flat on the wooden desk and felt its grain. I breathed out long and slow. And I kept telling myself, it's a wave, it peaks, then it drops. It peaked. It dropped. I wrote the paper. Afterwards I went to the campus clinic just to check, and they helped me find a counsellor.

qa.a: The hall had two hundred desks.

qa.q: How might other students in the hall have seen Nikita, if they noticed at all?
qa.a: They probably saw only someone pausing with hands flat on a desk, not the storm Nikita felt inside.

grounding: A young adult in an exam hall feels heat, tingling, a tight chest and an urge to escape, and gets through with slow breathing, touching something solid and remembering the wave passes.

passage:
In the university library in Valencia, Sami's pen stopped moving. Camila looked up from her notes and saw him gripping the table, breathing in fast gulps, his face grey. "I can't... my chest..."
Camila put her book down slowly. "I'm here," she said. "You're not alone." She kept her words short. She didn't tell him to relax. "Do you want to stay sitting, or go outside?"
He nodded toward the door. They walked to the courtyard bench. The air was cool. Camila breathed slowly beside him and waited. After a while his shoulders dropped and the colour came back to his face.
"Sorry," he said.
"Nothing to be sorry for." She paused. "Will you see the campus doctor this week? Just to check your heart's okay, and maybe talk to someone about these?"
Sami gave a shaky laugh. "Okay. If you come with me."

qa.q: Where did Camila and Sami go?
qa.a: They walked to the courtyard bench.

qa.q: What was Camila feeling, and how can you tell she stayed calm?
qa.a: Camila was probably alarmed but steady; she put her book down slowly, kept her words short and breathed slowly beside Sami.

qa.q: Why did Camila ask whether Sami wanted to sit or go outside?
qa.a: Letting Sami choose gave back some control when he felt trapped, which can ease panic more than being told what to do.

qa.q: What was the moment in the library like for Sami?
qa.a: Sami was frightened, gasping and grey-faced with a tight chest, and afterwards relieved and a little embarrassed.

grounding: A helper stays calm, uses short sentences, avoids telling the person to relax, lets them choose where to be, and afterwards encourages a check-up and support.

The community-centre hall was booming with drums when Pooja sank to the floor behind the stage curtain, hands over her chest. "It's happening again," she whispered.
Vishal crouched in front of her, not too close. "Okay. I'm with you." He kept it simple. "You're safe. Breathe out with me."
A girl from the troupe rushed over. "Just relax, Pooja!" Vishal shook his head at her gently and asked Pooja, "Here, or the quiet room?"
"Here," Pooja said. So they stayed on the floor, backs against the wall, Vishal breathing slowly and saying little. The drums went on. After some minutes, Pooja's hands unclenched.
Later, while the others packed up, Vishal said, "You said again. Has a doctor ever checked this?"
"No."
"Would you go this week? I'll help you find a counsellor too."
Pooja nodded, tired but steadier.

passage: For two years I built my life around not panicking. I took the stairs to the ninth floor so I wouldn't be trapped in the lift. I sat by the door in every meeting. I said no to the office trip to Goa and invented a family function. I told nobody. It felt shameful, like a weakness I had to hide, even though I'm Zubin, the one who fixes everyone's laptops. Last winter Sangeeta, who shares my desk pod, found me pale on the stairwell. I finally told her everything. She didn't laugh. She said, "That sounds exhausting. Have you seen anyone about it?" That question got me to a psychologist. Months of practice later, I still get the odd wave, but I take the lift most days now. Telling one person made it lighter to carry.

qa.q: Which floor did Zubin climb the stairs to?
qa.a: Zubin took the stairs to the ninth floor.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel about the panic before telling anyone?
qa.a: Zubin felt ashamed and secretive, treating it as a weakness to hide, even inventing a family function.

qa.q: What turned things around for Zubin?
qa.a: Telling Sangeeta, and her question about seeing someone, which led Zubin to a psychologist and months of practice.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta have seen Zubin on the stairwell?
qa.a: Sangeeta seemed concerned rather than judging, calling it exhausting and gently asking if Zubin had seen anyone.

grounding: A working adult plans life around avoiding panic and hides it in shame, and telling one person and getting professional help ease it.

Supervisor's notebook, private. Indu Ramaswamy, warehouse B.
Asif has asked to swap out of the cold-storage shift four times this month. He gets sharp when pressed about it and eats lunch alone in his car. I assumed he disliked the work. Today he came to me, stared at the floor and said he gets panic attacks in the cold room, with its heavy door, and has hidden it for over a year because he thought I'd think less of him. He looked ashamed.
I thanked him for telling me and promised it stays between us. I've moved him to the packing line for now. I gave him the number for our employee counselling service and said many people recover well with proper help. He seemed lighter walking out. I'll check in with him quietly next Friday.

qa.a: Asif felt ashamed and afraid of being thought less of; he stared at the floor, but seemed lighter afterwards.

On the farm outside Mehsana, Nilesh kicked the water bucket across the yard. "I'm not feeding the goats! Why do I always have to?"
"Don't you shout at me!" Bhavna shouted back, louder. "Pick that up right now!"
Nilesh's voice went higher. "You never listen!" The goats bleated. Both of them were red-faced, and the shouting climbed and climbed.
Then Bhavna heard her own voice ringing off the shed and stopped. She took a long breath. "We're both too angry to talk," she said quietly. "I'm going to sit by the well. We'll talk after."
Nilesh stood with his fists clenched, then slowly picked up the bucket. Later, sitting beside her on the well's edge, he said, "Rohit never feeds them. It's not fair." Bhavna nodded. "Then let's make a turn chart."

In their flat in Manchester, Soo-ah slammed the tablet on the sofa. "You're so unfair! Five more minutes!"
"Don't you dare slam things!" her mum, Nkechi, yelled from the kitchen. "That's it, no tablet all week!"
"I hate this house!" Soo-ah screamed, and her throat hurt from it. Her mum's face was as red as hers.
Then Nkechi put down the dish towel and stood very still. When she spoke again, her voice was low. "I'm shouting too. That's not helping either of us. I'm going to make tea, and we'll talk when we're calmer."
Soo-ah, braced for more yelling, didn't know what to do with the quiet. Twenty minutes later, on the sofa, she said, "Sorry I slammed it." Nkechi said, "Sorry I yelled. Let's work out the tablet rule together."

qa.a: The fight would likely have kept climbing, and Soo-ah would learn that shouting louder is how anger gets handled.

passage: I'm Gopika, and I sit two rows behind Madhav in Class 10. On Tuesday, Mr Kurian read out his test mark and said, "Maybe try opening a book this year." A few people laughed. I saw Madhav's neck go red, his jaw working, his fingers digging into the desk edge. He stood up so fast his chair scraped. I honestly thought he would shout something he couldn't take back. Instead he said, in a tight voice, "May I go to the washroom, sir?" and walked out. Through the window I saw him at the tap, splashing cold water on his face again and again. When he came back, his shoulders were down. After class he went up to Mr Kurian and said calmly, "That comment hurt. Can we talk about my marks another time?" I don't know what was going on in his head, but I know what he didn't say.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt when Jyoti first accused him?
qa.a: Tarun felt defensive and stung, since he had taken the money for Bebe's medicines.

grounding: Someone notices anger rising, says she needs a break, and returns later to talk about the problem without blame.
